sections.h2: How does probate work in Minnesota?
sections.html:
Minnesota probate follows Chapter 524, the state's version of the Uniform Probate Code. A court registrar opens an informal case from a verified application, or a judge hears a formal petition when someone objects or the situation is contested. In either track, the person appointed as personal representative gains the authority to collect assets, pay debts and deliver the remainder to the people entitled to it.

Under Minn. Stat. 524.3-302, the registrar can issue a written statement of informal probate once at least 120 hours have passed since the death. That informal probate is conclusive as to everyone until a formal testacy order replaces it. An application for informal probate or appointment must state the applicant's interest, the decedent's name, birthdate, date of death and domicile, and the names and addresses of the spouse, children, heirs and devisees, as Minn. Stat. 524.3-301 lists.

The clock for starting is long but not endless. Minn. Stat. 524.3-108 bars most informal and formal probate or appointment proceedings that start more than three years after the death. A will contest after informal probate may be filed within the later of 12 months from the informal probate or three years from the death.

sections.h2: Who can serve as personal representative of a Minnesota estate?
sections.html:
Section Minn. Stat. 524.3-203 ranks the people who may ask for appointment. A person named in a probated will comes first, followed by a surviving spouse who is also a devisee, other devisees, the surviving spouse, and other heirs. Any creditor gets a turn 45 days after the death, and a conservator who has not been discharged ranks after 90 days.

Someone with a right to letters in the spouse, devisee or heir ranks may nominate a qualified person instead, and anyone 18 or older can renounce the right in writing filed with the court. An objection to an appointment can be made only in a formal proceeding. When an heir or devisee with a substantial interest objects to someone other than the person named in the will, the court may appoint a person acceptable to the heirs and devisees holding more than half of the probable distributable value.

sections.h2: Can a Minnesota estate avoid probate?
sections.html:
Some small estates can. Thirty days after death, a successor may collect personal property by affidavit if the entire probate estate, measured at the date of death and reduced by liens and encumbrances, does not exceed $75,000 and no application for a personal representative is pending anywhere (Minn. Stat. 524.3-1201). A bank, a safe deposit company or a person holding the property must then release it against a certified death record and the affidavit. Motor vehicle titles can also be reissued the same way.

A second route is a summary proceeding. Minn. Stat. 524.3-1203 lets the court find that a decedent had no estate, or only exempt property and amounts owed for the property selection, spousal and child allowances, and certain expenses, and then assign that property to the people entitled without a full administration. The affidavit procedure in 524.3-1201 covers personal property, so ask the court administrator how a house in the estate should be handled.

  • Ask a title company or attorney whether the house is part of the probate estate at all, since a transfer on death deed or co-ownership can change the answer.
  • Count only the probate estate against the $75,000 figure, less liens and encumbrances.
  • Ask the court administrator in the county where the decedent lived which forms apply to your situation.

sections.h2: Can the personal representative sell an inherited Minnesota house?
sections.html:
Yes, usually. Minn. Stat. 524.3-715, clause 23, lets a personal representative sell, mortgage or lease any real or personal property of the estate, the homestead included, for cash or on credit, without the consent of any devisee or heir. Two limits apply: the property cannot have been specifically devised to a devisee or heir, and a homestead in which the surviving spouse takes an interest cannot be sold, mortgaged or leased without the spouse's written consent.

The homestead has its own descent rule in Minn. Stat. 524.2-402. With a surviving spouse and no descendants, it goes to the spouse. With descendants, the spouse takes a life interest and the descendants share the remainder. A homestead that passes to a spouse or descendants is exempt from debts that were not valid charges on it at the date of death, apart from certain state hospital and medical assistance claims.

Heirs who inherit a house they do not want to keep face the usual choices: list it with an agent, sell as-is for cash, or hold it while the estate is open. The same statute also lets the representative make repairs, insure the property, and pay taxes and reasonable administration costs from the estate.

sections.html:

sections.h2: How are creditors handled in a Minnesota probate?
sections.html:
After appointment of a general personal representative, notice goes out under the court administrator's direction by publication once a week for two successive weeks in a legal newspaper of the county. It tells creditors to present claims within four months of the notice or be barred. The personal representative must also serve a copy on each known and identified creditor within three months after the first publication (Minn. Stat. 524.3-801). A creditor is known when the representative has been told of the claim, when accessible financial records disclose it, or when a reasonably diligent search of those records would reveal it.

Under Minn. Stat. 524.3-803, claims that arose before death are barred unless presented within four months after the published notice, or within the later of four months after first publication or one month after service for creditors who were served. A one-year limit from the date of death applies whether or not notice was published, though state claims for medical assistance and similar benefits are not cut off at one year. A mortgage or other lien on estate property can still be enforced.

sections.h2: What taxes and paperwork apply when selling an inherited Minnesota home?
sections.html:
A deed of distribution by a personal representative is exempt from state deed tax under Minn. Stat. 287.22. When that deed is presented to the county auditor, Minn. Stat. 272.12 has the auditor enter the transfer on the books and mark the deed "transfer entered" so it can be recorded. A regular deed to a buyer gets the auditor's check for delinquent taxes first, and the recorder refuses an instrument without the auditor's notation. Any delinquent property tax therefore has to be paid before the deed can be recorded.

Two other rules touch inherited property. The seller disclosure requirements in sections 513.52 to 513.60 do not apply to a transfer to heirs or devisees of a decedent, according to Minn. Stat. 513.54. And on any sale for more than $3,000, a certificate of value goes to the county auditor when the deed is presented for recording (Minn. Stat. 272.115).

For estate tax questions, ask the Minnesota Department of Revenue or the estate's attorney whether a Minnesota return is needed for the estate's size, and obtain written confirmation before distributing the proceeds.

faqs.q: Do I always need probate to sell a house after a death in Minnesota?
faqs.a: Not always. A very small estate can use an affidavit to collect personal property, and a house that is not part of the probate estate needs no personal representative. A house titled only in the decedent's name is part of the estate, and the personal representative signs the sale documents.

faqs.q: What is the Minnesota small estate limit?
faqs.a: $75,000. The figure covers the whole probate estate at the date of death, wherever located, less liens and encumbrances. Thirty days must pass after the death, and no application or petition to appoint a personal representative can be pending.

faqs.q: How long do creditors have to file claims against a Minnesota estate?
faqs.a: Generally four months after the published notice, or one month after service if that is later, and always within one year of death for claims that arose before death. Claims that arise at or after death have their own four-month periods.

faqs.q: Is there a deadline to open probate in Minnesota?
faqs.a: Yes. Most informal and formal probate or appointment proceedings must begin within three years of the death. A special administrator can still be appointed after that period for limited purposes such as collecting assets.

faqs.q: Is deed tax owed when an estate deeds a house to the heirs?
faqs.a: No. A deed of distribution by a personal representative is on the list of instruments exempt from Minnesota state deed tax. The deed still goes through the county auditor before the recorder accepts it.
